answer.rationale:
Constraints eliminate the strongest-looking precedent first: memory_b1 (rollback) is the cleanest historical fix but compliance has ruled the security patch non-revertible, so rollback is off the table regardless of how well it worked on day 18. The signal that the degradation is confined to the primary region points at memory_b2 (regional failover), which is why that is the one memory worth spending the verification budget on. The consolidated summary of b2 is thin in exactly the way that matters here: it says traffic shifted cleanly and error rates recovered within minutes, but it does not say whether the March degradation was on the write path, what the write volume was at the time, or whether any in-flight writes were lost or reconciled after the shift. A failover that was clean during a read-heavy or low-volume period is weak evidence for a failover at settlement peak with heavy writes, where replication lag between primary and secondary is the dominant risk to the stated objective of not losing customer writes. So I want the original record to see if b2 was actually a write-path event and whether write-loss was assessed or merely unobserved.

Intent, pending that record: regional failover, but scoped as a small guarded test rather than a full region cutover — shift a bounded slice of write traffic, confirm replication lag and write acknowledgement on the secondary, and hold the rest until the slice is clean. This keeps the one available intervention reversible instead of betting the settlement window on a summary sentence.

Downstream value risk: a broad failover at peak can convert a latency problem into a durability problem, and lost settlement writes are far more costly and less recoverable than elevated p99. There is also a compounding risk that a failover masks the underlying cause, so the primary region carries an undiagnosed defect into the next window.

Uncertainty I am explicitly not collapsing: I have not established the cause of the write-path climb. A 90-minute ramp beginning roughly contemporaneously with a 2-hour-old release is suspicious — the release may be the driver even though it cannot be reverted, in which case failover moves the same code onto fresh hardware and buys only temporary relief. memory_b5 offers a plausible alternative (relieving primary contention by moving reads off it) that carries no write-loss exposure, and memory_b4 (circuit breakers) is a containment option if a dependency turns out to be the source. If the b2 record shows the March event was not write-heavy, or shows write-loss was never actually verified, I switch to route_read_replicas as the safer single intervention and defer failover to the next window with proper lag checks.
